content: Glanders is an infectious disease that primarily affects horses, mules, and donkeys. It can also infect other animals, including dogs, cats, and goats. The disease is caused by the bacterium Burkholderia mallei, which is typically transmitted through the ingestion of contaminated food or water. The clinical manifestations of glanders include the development of nodular lesions in the lungs and ulceration of the mucous membranes in the upper respiratory tract. In its acute form, the disease presents with symptoms such as coughing, fever, and the release of infectious nasal discharge. This is often followed by septicemia and death within a matter of days. In the chronic form, nasal and subcutaneous nodules form, which eventually ulcerate. Death may occur within months, and animals that survive can become carriers of the disease. Glanders is endemic in regions such as Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Central America, and South America. However, it has been eradicated in North America, Australia, and most of Europe through rigorous surveillance, culling of infected animals, and import restrictions. The bacterium Burkholderia mallei is zoonotic, meaning it can infect humans. Transmission to humans occurs through direct contact with infected animals, with the bacterium entering the body via skin abrasions, nasal or oral mucosal surfaces, or inhalation. Due to its high mortality rate in humans and the small number of organisms required to establish an infection, Burkholderia mallei is considered a potential biological warfare or bioterrorism agent. Its closely related species, Burkholderia pseudomallei, which causes melioidosis, is also regarded as a potential bioweapon. During World War I, glanders was reportedly used as a biological weapon by German agents to infect Russian horses and mules on the Eastern Front, disrupting troop and supply movements. Human cases in Russia increased during and after the war. During World War II, the Japanese deliberately infected horses, civilians, and prisoners of war with B. mallei at the Pingfang Institute in China. The United States studied the bacterium as a potential biological weapon in 1943–44 but did not weaponize it. The Soviet Union is also believed to have explored B. mallei as a biological warfare agent after World War II. Images from the Public Health Image Library (PHIL) depict the colonial morphology of Burkholderia mallei bacteria grown on various media, such as sheep’s blood agar (SBA) and chocolate agar. These images also include the colonial morphology of Burkholderia thailandensis, a related species, grown on sheep’s blood agar.
